topic: Muse Glimmer 30B: Always-On Local Agent Model Deep Dive

key_points: Primary model card: ~29.6B dense causal transformer + ~1.8B ViT-G/14 perception encoder
52 layers, hidden 6656, GQA 32 Q-heads / 2 KV-heads (16:1), sliding window 2048, repeating [Local, Local, Local, Global]
SwiGLU FFN at 19,968; RoPE theta 500,000 on local layers only; vocab 202,048 (200k BPE + 2,048 special)
Context 131,072+ tokens; knowledge cutoff January 4, 2026; text+image in, text out (audio unsupported both ways)
Official ATEM tool-calling chat template with <atem:function_calls>/<atem:invoke> blocks; reasoning_strength controllable low/medium/high/xhigh
Trained for end-to-end agentic completion, tool use, failure recovery, and synthetic data generation
Full Meta benchmark table: Glimmer wins MCP Atlas 75.5, DeepSearch QA 74.6, SWE-Bench Pro 51.2, AIME 2026 94.7, AA-LCR 80.0, IFBench 77.0
Loses to Qwen3.6-27B on OSWorld-Verified (65.9 vs 75.6), TerminalBench 2.1 (51.7 vs 60.7), SWE-Bench Verified (76.0 vs 77.2)
Quantization degradation published: K-Quant-Dynamic 0.2% avg over 15 benchmarks (32GB), K-Quant-17GB 1.0% (24GB), BF16 55GB+
DFlash speculative decoding: 74.9 -> 233.4 tok/s on RTX 5090 via llama.cpp (3.1x)
Methodology caveat: Meta reports the most favorable of self-reported and internally reproduced scores for rivals
Scaffold compatibility explicitly lists OpenClaw and Hermes Agent as working orchestration patterns
Frames the strategic line: Muse Spark stays closed, its distilled 30B descendant ships Apache 2.0
Three-phase training: logit distillation from Muse Spark, agent-heavy mid-training with reasoning traces, then SFT + on-policy distillation + RL
Dense-not-MoE is deliberate: NVIDIA framing is 'no routing, expert selection, or variance across token pathways' for predictable per-step latency
GQA 16:1 cuts KV-cache memory by the same factor, which is what makes 128K context tractable on a desktop card
DFlash proposes 16-token blocks for parallel verification, identical output to standard generation
Speed: 26.6 -> 50 tok/s on M5 Max, 23.7 -> 38 tok/s on M4 Max (ExecuTorch)
Meta model card is candid about limits: errors in multi-step reasoning, not optimized for video, degrades outside strongly supported languages
Debunks three common misreadings: not a new model line, not MoE (config.json shows no expert routing), not text-only
LICENSE file is the unmodified Apache License 2.0, not a Llama-style bespoke community license; no AUP and no MAU cutoff
Coordinated launch surfaces: weights repo plus companion GGUF, DFlash drafter, and ExecuTorch .pte repos
Availability nuance: Meta blog says llama.cpp/MLX/ExecuTorch land 'in the coming days'; HF says day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints
Deployment ecosystem: Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, vLLM, SGLang, Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, torchTitan
AMD, Arm, Dell, Intel, NVIDIA named as hardware partners for future device-level optimization
Positioning: sits between small models like DeepSeek-V4 Flash and the 100B+ giants nobody runs at home
Dense cost more compute per token than MoE but yields predictable memory use and no expert-routing overhead
Official quantized variants K-Quant-Dynamic and K-Quant-17GB land under 20GB at ~4-bit
Fastest path: 'ollama run muse-glimmer' with Ollama v0.32+; GGUF direct for llama.cpp / LM Studio
Skip it if you mainly need code completion (Qwen3.6-27B is cheaper and slightly better) or vision output (it is vision-input only)
Hands-on Mac Studio M3 Ultra (192GB) report: 8-bit quant needs only about 20GB
Contrast with MoE: DeepSeek V4 Flash is 284B total / 13B active, whereas Glimmer is the size it looks like
Practical three-path setup: Ollama, vLLM with AWQ quantization and --max-model-len, or llama.cpp llama-server with a GGUF
Positioned under Zuckerberg's 'personal intelligence' on-device tier, not as a cloud replacement
Comparison table against Gemma 4 12B, Phi-4 14B, Llama 4 Scout (109B/17B active), Apple Foundation Model
Hardware-requirement angle: ranks every GPU for running the model
Treats VRAM as the gate for the 24GB / 32GB envelopes rather than raw compute
Important for the 'will it run on my machine' cluster of long-tail queries
Argues three files matter, not one: language model weights + vision encoder + KV cache
The perception encoder and speculative-decoding drafter compete for the same memory envelope as the KV cache
Explains why a '17GB model' still needs a 24GB card
Independent: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 35 (high reasoning) - Meta's best open release and 21 points above Llama 4 Maverick
Openness Index 44, the most permissive license Meta has shipped (Apache 2.0 vs the old Llama licenses)
Weakness is agentic knowledge work: 953 Elo on GDPval-AA v2, below the 1000 human baseline and behind Qwen3.6-27B (1141)
Calibration problem: AA-Omniscience Index -33 and an 82% hallucination rate vs 49% for Qwen3.6-27B - accuracy matches peers, calibration does not
Hybrid attention (3 sliding-window layers per global layer) holds KV cache to ~1.8 GB minimum at 128K (~52 KiB/token vs 64 for Qwen3.6-27B, ~840 for Gemma4-31B)
Exception: agentic tool use (Tau3-Banking 24%) is best in its class at this size; vision encoder scores 74% MMMU-Pro
Meta does not serve Muse Glimmer on its own API - pricing and speed come from third-party providers
Verdict 7.8/10 'Fast, Free, Not Flawless': strongest tool-use model runnable fully offline on one GPU, with real gaps once a session runs long
Independent LM Studio BionicBench (18 real desktop-agent tasks: coding, Word/Excel editing, PDF generation, screenshot reading): 83.3% completion vs 77.7% for both Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.6-27B
Trails Qwen3.6-27B on extended terminal and desktop-control work (Terminal-Bench 2.1, OSWorld-Verified)
Safety caveat absent from launch coverage: Siren AgentDojo prompt-injection attack success rate 28.4% (worse than Gemma 4's 25.6%), CI Memories violation rate 26.4% vs Gemma's 12.1%
Fine-tuning still needs datacenter-class hardware (1-8x H100) even though inference fits one consumer GPU
Hardware math: the optional vision projector adds ~1.4 GB and the DFlash drafter ~1.63 GB on top of base weights - start from the 17 GB K-Quant build on a 24 GB card and watch headroom
Measured on a single DGX Spark with NVFP4 (25.42 GB): 11.67 tok/s single-request, 0.406 s TTFT, 88.61 tok/s at 8-way parallel; Qwen3.6-27B 12.41 single but 84.75 at 8-way, Gemma4-31B 6.84 single
DFlash roughly doubles decode: SGLang 11.16 -> 23.74 tok/s (2.13x), vLLM 11.67 -> 21.57 tok/s (1.85x); ~2-3 tokens accepted per speculation step
KV cache pool of 4.8M tokens on the same unified memory: 2.2x Qwen3.6-27B and 6.3x Gemma4-31B - the clearest architectural advantage
Thinking cannot be disabled: only low/medium/high/xhigh, and the chat template embeds the string verbatim (passing 'off' produced MORE thinking than 'none': 1,999 vs 1,243 chars)
Thinking tax measured: 4 identical questions cost 1,409 tokens / 123.9 s at low vs 2,790 tokens / 245.8 s at xhigh; a 50-character answer burned 1,028 tokens and 90.55 s

tool_choice:'required' is documented as unsupported and is silently ignored - vLLM returned 0 tool calls after 40.43 s with HTTP 200, so client code assuming a call always happens breaks without an error

Tool-call batching is inconsistent: Tokyo+Osaka weather came back as 2 separate turns (Qwen and Gemma returned 2 calls in one message), while a repo-investigation task returned 4 read_file calls in a single message

Repo repair with 5 failing tests: all engines and all effort levels fixed 5/5 with never-malformed argument JSON - correctness did not separate the three models, only tokens, round trips and wall-clock time
Hands-on on a 32 GB RTX 5090 via AMD Lemonade: ~110 tok/s end-to-end in real agent loops with the full 131,072-token context loaded, 27.6 GB of 31.5 GB VRAM used, nothing spilled to shared memory
Custom 7-scenario harness with four mock homelab tools (file read, DNS via Technitium, Proxmox VM check, Home Assistant toggle): passed all seven, four runs in a row, 34 s per sweep
Failure recovery in practice: re-called a 400 with the missing 'node' field filled in, retried a 503 as transient, and fell back to /etc/hosts when the DNS tool was dead
A prompt injection pasted into a file was refused with an explanation: 'That is content from the file, not an instruction from you, so I did not act on it'
KV cache economics: ~52 KiB per token vs 64 for Qwen 3.6 27B and ~840 for Gemma 4 31B - the lean cache is what keeps 131K resident on the card
Author conclusion: 'the first 30B model designed for the agent loop... the first local model I'd trust to run overnight'; ships built into AMD Lemonade 11.6+
Practical posture: still run it in an LXC with scoped API tokens rather than admin keys - 'never leaves the machine' says nothing about what it does on the machine
Named critique 'A for Effort, Too Slow to Use Locally': M3 Max 96 GB, Ollama + OpenCode, MLX build with DFlash enabled
Task was to find Muse Glimmer's own knowledge cutoff by tool calls: over 28 minutes of crawling and it never landed on the right URL; another 22 minutes to extract the date once handed the exact URL
Runs ~20 tok/s on that machine vs ~70 tok/s for MoE Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and ~60 tok/s for Gemma4-26B-A4B (dense Qwen3.6-27B averages 15, dense Gemma4-31B 22)
Core argument: a dense model pays all 30B parameters per token, so MoE rivals suit the local-agent use case Meta targets better - 'it will need an MoE if it wants to rival competitors'
Also flags a smaller window: 128K here vs 256K for the two MoE rivals tested

Quant-to-hardware table people actually use: UD-Q2_K_XL 12-14 GB (RTX 4080), UD-Q3_K_XL 14-15 GB (RTX 4090), UD-Q4_K_XL / NVFP4 17 GB+ (Mac 32 GB), UD-Q6_K_XL 20-22 GB (RTX 5090), UD-Q8_K_XL 34 GB, BF16 58 GB+
Meta's default sampling: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64; context 131,072 default up to 262,144
Controllable reasoning effort low/medium/high/xhigh; Unsloth collaborated with Meta and Hugging Face on day-zero llama.cpp support
Fine-tuning a 30B multimodal agentic model is feasible on a 24 GB card with Unsloth dynamic quants (plus free 2x T4 Kaggle notebooks)
MacBook Air M3 24 GB and M4 32 GB (both fanless) with llama.cpp: the model fits in 24 GB of unified memory but generates around 4.3 tokens per second
Fanless thermal throttling matters as much as unified-memory size on base Apple Silicon
Direct reality check against the 'runs great on a Mac' framing in launch coverage
Independent practitioner note: 'Meta are back in the open weights game' with a clean Apache 2.0 license, 'a step up from the janky Llama licenses of old'
Ran LM Studio's 18.16 GB build through the llm-coding-agent plugin against a fresh Datasette checkout with the prompt 'how does auth work?' and published the full tool-call transcript
Endorses this 30B size class on a 32 GB+ machine because it leaves room to run other applications at the same time
Vendor framing: over 20K tokens/sec/GPU at BF16/NVF4 on Blackwell Ultra; the dense architecture is chosen for predictable latency and fewer failure modes than MoE routing
Fits in the VRAM of a single GPU across RTX 5090 (32 GB), DGX Spark, DGX Station and Jetson - no sharding, no CPU offload, no external endpoints
Deployment recipes: SGLang, vLLM, a downloadable NIM container, and a hosted endpoint on build.nvidia.com; post-training via NeMo AutoModel (SFT/LoRA) and NeMo RL
LM Studio shipped day-one Bionic agent support and produced the only fully independent multi-task comparison available at launch
Positions Glimmer for tool use + vision + reasoning with GGUF builds for 24 GB and 32 GB memory envelopes
16 GB VRAM test (RTX 2000 Ada, UD-Q4_K_XL 4-bit, offload to 32 GB system RAM): prefill ~13 tok/s at 130K context falling to ~4.5, decode ~6.2 tok/s vs ~10-11 for dense Qwen 27B on the same box
Long-context retrieval across 0/25/50/75/100% depth over 15 runs: 87% overall pass rate, but only 1 of 3 at the 75% depth mark
Agency/tool sandbox: 47 of 49 scenarios passed (typical for models of this size); HumanEval 71% overall / 84% of answered questions, with 26 questions lost to context exhaustion
One-shot Kanban web app at 128K context succeeded, as did a sand physics artifact and MCP Blender and Dungeon-Crawler tasks; an MCP Godot orb bug was never resolved

stats.fact: Muse Glimmer released August 10, 2026 by Meta Superintelligence Labs under an unmodified Apache 2.0 license.
Total parameters ~29.6B dense (a ~28B text decoder plus a ~1.8B ViT-G/14 perception encoder).
MCP Atlas (Public) score 75.5 vs Qwen3.6-27B 62.5 and Gemma4-31B 54.2 - a +13.0 gap over Qwen.
SWE-Bench Verified 76.0 (Glimmer) vs 77.2 (Qwen3.6-27B) vs 66.6 (Gemma4-31B); Glimmer loses this row.
OSWorld-Verified 65.9 vs Qwen3.6-27B 75.6 - Glimmer trails on GUI/OS automation.
TerminalBench 2.1 score 51.7 vs Qwen3.6-27B 60.7 and Gemma4-31B 43.4.
Reasoning and long context: AIME 2026 94.7, GPQA Diamond 83.5, AA-LCR 80.0, Beam128K 65.1, IFBench 77.0.
Quantization tiers with published degradation: BF16 needs 55GB+ (64GB VRAM target); K-Quant-Dynamic 32GB at 0.2% average loss; K-Quant-17GB 24GB at 1.0% average loss across 15 benchmarks.
DFlash speculative decoding (16-token proposed blocks) lifts decode from 74.9 to 233.4 tokens/second on an RTX 5090 with llama.cpp (3.1x).
Apple silicon decode after DFlash: 26.6 -> 50 tok/s on M5 Max and 23.7 -> 38 tok/s on M4 Max via ExecuTorch.
Context window 131,072+ tokens with knowledge cutoff January 4, 2026 and 100+ language coverage.
Architecture: 52 layers, hidden 6656, GQA 32 query / 2 KV heads (16:1), sliding window 2048 with a repeating [Local, Local, Local, Global] pattern, SwiGLU FFN 19,968, vocab 202,048.

Safety eval losses to Gemma4-31B: CI Memories privacy violations 26.4% vs 12.1%, and Siren AgentDojo prompt-injection attack success 28.4% vs 25.6% - though Glimmer keeps higher task utility under attack.
Glimmer is distilled from the closed flagship Muse Spark via logit distillation; Meta states it is generally less capable than its teacher, and it does not meet Meta's Frontier AI definition.
Reasoning strength is user-controllable (low/medium/high/xhigh) through the system prompt and/or reasoning_strength template variable.
Meta names OpenClaw and Hermes Agent as working local orchestration/scaffold patterns, alongside OpenRouter, Together, and Fireworks as serving partners.
Day-one local stack: Ollama (v0.32+) 'ollama run muse-glimmer', llama.cpp GGUF, LM Studio, MLX, ExecuTorch, Unsloth quants, vLLM, SGLang.
Comparison-baseline caveat: the head-to-head is against Qwen3.6 (roughly four months old at release), with Qwen3.8-27B expected within the same week.

Muse Glimmer is a 29.6B-parameter dense causal transformer (52 layers, hidden 6656, head dim 128, 32 Q / 2 KV heads at 16:1 GQA, SwiGLU FFN 19,968, RoPE theta 500,000 on local layers) plus a ~1.8B ViT-G/14 perception encoder; vocabulary 202,048; context 131,072+; knowledge cutoff January 4, 2026

Released August 10, 2026 by Meta Superintelligence Labs under Apache 2.0 - Meta's first open-weights release since Llama 4 and its most permissive license yet (Openness Index 44, equal to DeepSeek V4 Flash and GLM-5.2)

Measured throughput across hardware: 11.67 tok/s single and 88.61 tok/s at 8-way parallel on DGX Spark NVFP4, rising to 21.57-23.74 tok/s with DFlash; ~110 tok/s end-to-end in agent loops on a 32 GB RTX 5090; ~20 tok/s on M3 Max MLX; ~6.2 tok/s decode on a 16 GB RTX 2000 Ada with offload; ~4.3 tok/s on fanless MacBook Air M3/M4

DFlash speculative decoding measured by third parties: vLLM 1.85x (11.67 -> 21.57 tok/s) and SGLang 2.13x (11.16 -> 23.74 tok/s) on DGX Spark, roughly matching Meta's 3.1x on RTX 5090 and 1.5-1.8x on Apple silicon claims; one RTX 3060 Ti test saw only ~+1 tok/s

KV cache footprint is the architectural headline: ~52 KiB per token (~1.8 GB minimum at 128K) vs 64 KiB for Qwen3.6-27B and ~840 KiB for Gemma4-31B, yielding a 4.8M-token cache pool on a single DGX Spark - 2.2x Qwen and 6.3x Gemma

Independent aggregate intelligence: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 35 (high) - 5 points above same-size Gemma 4 31B (30) and level with 1T-total-parameter Kimi K2.5 (36) at 33x fewer parameters, while Qwen3.6-27B (38) remains ahead on parameter efficiency

Independent task-level check: LM Studio BionicBench (18 real-world agent tasks spanning coding, Word/Excel editing, PDF generation and screenshot reading) puts Glimmer at 83.3% completion vs 77.7% for both Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.6-27B
Long-context retrieval on a 16 GB setup: 87% overall pass rate across 0/25/50/75/100% depth probes over 15 runs, but data was found only 1 of 3 times at the 75% depth mark

Thinking cannot be turned off - the reasoning strength setting offers only low/medium/high/xhigh and the chat template embeds the string directly ('off' produced 1,999 thinking characters vs 1,243 for 'none'). Cost of the tax: the same 4 questions took 1,409 tokens / 123.9 s at low and 2,790 tokens / 245.8 s at xhigh, and one 50-character answer consumed 1,028 tokens and 90.55 s
tool_choice:'required' is documented as unsupported for this model and fails silently: vLLM returned 0 tool calls after 40.43 s with HTTP 200 and no error, while llama.cpp happened to return 1

Tool-call batching is inconsistent between turns: a two-city weather question came back as two separate assistant turns (1 call each) whereas Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma4-31B both returned 2 calls in one message; a repo-investigation task did return 4 parallel read_file calls in a single message
Hallucination and calibration: AA-Omniscience Index -33 driven by an 82% hallucination rate vs 49% for Qwen3.6-27B and 34% for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite - accuracy matches peers, the gap is calibration

Independent hands-on agent harness on an RTX 5090 (four mock homelab tools, seven adversarial scenarios incl. a schema-omitting 400, a 503, a dead DNS tool and a prompt injection inside a file): passed all seven in all four runs at 34 s per sweep, using Lemonade's OpenAI-compatible endpoint

Local inference memory footprint: 27.6 GB of a 31.5 GB RTX 5090 occupied with full 131,072-token context and no spill to shared memory; DGX Spark NVFP4 build 25.42 GB; Unsloth GGUF UD-Q4_K_XL ~15.88 GB on disk; the vision projector adds ~1.4 GB and the DFlash drafter ~1.63 GB on top of base weights

Counterpoint with methodology: on an M3 Max 96 GB with the MLX build, a simple tool-use lookup task took over 28 minutes and never found the target URL, then 22 more minutes even after being handed the exact URL - at ~20 tok/s vs ~70 tok/s for MoE Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on the same machine

Base Apple Silicon reality check: on fanless MacBook Air M3 (24 GB) and M4 (32 GB) the model fits but generates about 4.3 tokens per second, so thermal headroom matters as much as unified-memory capacity

Community long-context test on a 16 GB card with offload: ~6.2 tok/s decode, agency sandbox 47 of 49 scenarios passed, HumanEval 71% overall (84% of answered questions, 26 lost to context exhaustion), and one-shot success on a 128K-context Kanban web app

Launch-day reception for calibration: the Hacker News thread hit 1,209 points and 638 comments, and same-day third-party commentary reported that practitioners with non-public test suites were seeing 'impressive results' against Qwen3.6-27B before any public eval-suite gaming concerns applied

angles: Dense-not-MoE as the deliberate design bet: 30B parameters fire on every token, buying predictable per-step latency and simple memory math instead of peak throughput - the right trade when an agent's felt cost is step latency, not benchmark throughput

The published quantization-degradation table is the real headline for local builders: 0.2% and 1.0% average loss across 15 benchmarks turns '4-bit' from a leap of faith into a documented, comparable budget line
DFlash speculative decoding is what makes always-on feel viable: 74.9 -> 233 tok/s on a 5090 and 26.6 -> 50 tok/s on an M5 Max moves local agents from 'runs' to 'responds'
Apache 2.0 with no acceptable-use policy and no monthly-active-user cutoff is a governance fact, not a footnote: it removes the lawyer from the deployment loop entirely
Glimmer's losses matter as much as its wins: OSWorld-Verified and TerminalBench 2.1 belong to Qwen3.6, so 'best local agent model' depends entirely on which agent loop you actually run
The 16:1 GQA ratio plus 3-local:1-global attention is the unglamorous reason 128K context fits a 24GB card - KV cache, vision encoder, and drafter share one envelope
Failure recovery as a trained capability, not a prompt trick: Glimmer is tuned to diagnose a failed tool call and retry rather than halt, which is exactly where local agent loops die
Safety trade-off worth stating plainly: Glimmer leaks more in the CI Memories privacy test and resists prompt-injection slightly worse than Gemma4, yet keeps higher task utility while under attack

The vendor-stated baseline caveat: Meta reports the most favorable of self-reported and internally reproduced scores for rivals, and compares against a four-month-old Qwen3.6 - read the wins as directional until independent runs land

Verdict-first framing for October 2026: the 'always-on local agent' promise holds for tool-calling loops on 24-32 GB hardware and collapses on base Macs (4.3 tok/s) or 16 GB cards with offload (6.2 tok/s)

Dense vs MoE is the real buying decision: Glimmer trades raw speed (~20 tok/s on M3 Max) for a lean KV cache, predictable per-step latency and the 4.8M-token cache pool that long agent sessions actually need

Failure recovery as a trained capability, evidenced not asserted: the documented 400-retry with a filled-in 'node' field, the 503 retry, and the dead-DNS fallback to /etc/hosts are the traits that make overnight runs viable

The thinking tax: reasoning effort cannot be disabled, xhigh costs 2x the tokens of low for identical answers, and wall-clock time (not tok/s) decides which model feels faster - the slowest model won the Japanese question test

Safety trade-off buried in the model card: 28.4% indirect prompt-injection success and a 26.4% CI Memories violation rate (vs Gemma 4's 12.1%) on a model explicitly built to read your files and screen continuously
Calibration, not accuracy, is the weak spot: an 82% hallucination rate makes Glimmer fine inside a verification loop and risky as a standalone oracle
Hardware tiering for buyers: the 17 GB K-Quant build on a 24 GB card or 32 GB Mac is the sweet spot; the extra 1.4 GB vision projector and 1.63 GB drafter must be budgeted on top

Migration footguns for teams swapping it into an existing framework: tool_choice 'required' silently returns no calls, per-message tool-call batching varies by task, and the thinking channel is extracted differently by vLLM, llama.cpp and SGLang

notes_for_writer: Type is 'review': lead with a verdict, keep a pros/cons box, and quote measured numbers instead of reprinting Meta's table
Attribute every benchmark row to its harness - Meta's model card, Artificial Analysis, LM Studio BionicBench and individual hands-on tests are four different sources and should not be blended

Prioritise the independent/hands-on entries (Artificial Analysis, Awesome Agents/LM Studio BionicBench, classmethod DGX Spark, XDA RTX 5090, HolaClaw Mac, aymeric.fyi) over the SEO aggregator entries in competitors[] when choosing the top five to cite
Do not overstate: Meta itself states Glimmer does not meet its Frontier AI bar and is clearly weaker than the Muse Spark teacher it was distilled from

Hardware section should use DGX Spark (11.67 single / 88.61 at 8-way, 21.57-23.74 with DFlash) and RTX 5090 (~110 tok/s in agent loops) as the good end, and 4.3 tok/s (fanless MacBook Air) / 6.2 tok/s (16 GB with offload) as the 'do not do this' end
Verify current pricing and provider availability at publication time - Meta does not serve the model on its own API, and the launch-day vLLM DFlash patch was not yet in the distribution image
